'''John "Jack" Francis Gunion''' (born 21 July 1943 in [[Washington, DC]])<ref>biographical information from ''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004</ref> is an American physicist, specializing in theoretical [[high energy physics]].

Gunion received in 1965 his bachelor's degree from [[Cornell University]] and in 1970 his Ph.D. from the [[University of California, San Diego]].<ref>{{cite web|website=UC San Diego Library Catalog|title=''Redemption of the dual description of production processes by unitarity. The relevance of the eikonal model'' by John Francis Gunion, 1970 Ph.D. dissertation|url=http://roger.ucsd.edu/search~S9?/aGunion/agunion/1%2C3%2C5%2CE/frameset&FF=agunion+j+f+john+francis+1943&3%2C3%2C}}</ref> As a postdoc he was from 1970 to 1972 at [[SLAC]] and from 1972 to 1973 at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. From 1973 to 1975 he was an assistant professor at the [[University of Pittsburgh]].<ref>{{cite web|title=John Gunion|website=U. C. Davis Physics Department|url=http://physics.ucdavis.edu/people/faculty/john-gunion}}</ref> In 1978 he moved to the [[University of California, Davis]] and remained there, retiring in 2017 as professor emeritus.<ref name=SakuraiPrize>{{cite web|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Gunion&first_nm=John&year=2017|title=2017 J. J. Sakurai Prize, John Gunion|website=APS Physics}}</ref>

He led the High Energy Physics Theory Group of the [[United States Department of Energy]] and was one of the initiators of the High Energy Frontier Theory Initiative (HEFTI).<ref name=SakuraiPrize/>

{{blockquote|As a result of his early work establishing the importance of the two-photon and four-lepton search modes for detecting a [[Standard Model]] [[Higgs boson]] and the detector properties needed to exploit them, Dr. Gunion was made a member of the [[Large Hadron Collider]] [[Compact Muon Solenoid]] (CMS) collaboration and was coauthor on the CMS Higgs discovery paper in which these modes played key roles.<ref name=SakuraiPrize/>}}

He coauthored, with three collaborators, an important monograph on the physics of the Higgs boson. He is the author or coauthor of hundreds of scientific articles and has an [[h-index]] of 100. He is currently working on Higgs physics beyond the Standard Model and [[supersymmetry]] with a focus on future collider detections of such physics.<ref name=SakuraiPrize/>

From 1974 to 1978 he was a Sloan Fellow and in 1989 he was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref name=SakuraiPrize/> In 2000 he was Schrödinger Professor at the Schrödinger Institute of the [[University of Vienna]].<ref>{{cite web|author=Grimus, Walter|title=List of "Schrödinger Guest Professors" (Samoil as a "Schrödinger Guest Professor" in Vienna|date=23 May 2018|url=http://indico.utef.cvut.cz/indico/event/6/session/8/material/0/0.pdf}}</ref> He is a member of the American Association for the Advancement of Science. In 2017 he, together with three collaborators, received the [[Sakurai Prize]] for "instrumental contributions to the theory of the properties, reactions, and signatures of the Higgs boson".<ref name=SakuraiPrize/>
